strengths: MU-Mis addresses a useful practical setting: unlearning requires only the pretrained model and forgetting data, without retained examples or stored training trajectories. The class-dependent input-sensitivity objective is an interesting methodological idea.

The class-removal results show promising utility preservation. On CIFAR-100, MU-Mis achieves 76.32% retained accuracy and 0% forget accuracy, compared with 76.91% retained accuracy after retraining. The face-recognition results are also competitive.

The loss ablation provides concrete support for combining both terms: retained accuracy improves from 60.45% with target-sensitivity minimization alone to 76.32%, while maintaining 0% forget accuracy. Retraining comparisons, timing measurements, and appendix analyses are useful additions.
weaknesses: The central derivation in Section 3.2 is mathematically unsound as presented. Differentiating through training omits derivatives of the loss gradient and the dependence of intermediate weights on training inputs. Furthermore, g_k g_k'^T is not generally symmetric for vector-valued outputs, so the asserted equality C_k = S_k does not follow. Small individual cross-sample terms also do not establish that their sum is negligible.

The connection between the surrogate and actual deletion remains unsupported. Sensitivity to infinitesimal input perturbations does not establish the effect of removing a training example. Additionally, the analyzed sum of unsquared non-target sensitivities becomes a single randomly sampled squared sensitivity in the implemented objective, changing the relative weighting without adequate justification or ablation.

The privacy evaluation is insufficient. MIA reports only the fraction of forgotten examples classified as members, without false-positive calibration or attack-discrimination results. Retrained models receive 94–95.4% membership scores in the random-subset and Sea settings. These measurements cannot establish successful information removal, and treating lower membership rates as uniformly better does not assess indistinguishability from retraining.

The random-subset experiment provides little evidence beyond leaving the model unchanged. In Table 5, both the original model and MU-Mis have 94.67% retained accuracy and 100% forget accuracy; MIA changes only from 95% to 94%, matching retraining. More discriminating evaluations are needed to demonstrate removal of individual-sample influence.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Numerical stopping thresholds and their selection procedure are missing, despite their central role in controlling forgetting. Algorithm 1 never accumulates the current loss used for stopping and places its purported maximum-iteration loop inside an unbounded repeat. Baseline configurations and evaluation splits are insufficiently specified, and code release is only promised.

The evidence does not support consistent, significant superiority. Experiments use only ResNet18, a small selection of deletion targets, and one random-subset size. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported; the CIFAR-100 retained-accuracy improvement over SSD is only 0.26 percentage points. Broader ablations and robustness across deletion sizes are needed.
